pick.headline: CIA station chief William Buckley kidnapped in Beirut
pick.summary: On March 16, 1984, William Buckley, the CIA's station chief in Beirut, was kidnapped by Islamic Jihad.
pick.significance: Buckley died in captivity after torture. Efforts to free him and other hostages helped drive the Reagan administration into the Iran-Contra arms deals.
pick.fbis: The Middle East & Africa Daily Report of March 16, 1984, noted, in its review, Radio Free Lebanon's report that three unidentified gunmen kidnapped "a U.S. Embassy official, William Buckley" outside his home on March 16, amid items on the Beirut cease-fire and the Iran-Iraq war.

alternates.headline: Red Brigades kidnap Aldo Moro
alternates.summary: On March 16, 1978, the Red Brigades kidnapped former Italian Prime Minister Aldo Moro in Rome, killing his five bodyguards.
alternates.significance: Moro was murdered after 55 days. The case shook Italy and raised lasting questions about the security services' handling of the search.
alternates.fbis: The Soviet Union Daily Report of March 17, 1978, listed under West Europe "Italian Leader Moro's Kidnaping in Rome Reported", with the Italian Interior Ministry cited, a call for a general strike, and Moscow commentaries calling it a "Reactionary Provocation" and blaming right-wing forces.

alternates.headline: Iraq gasses the Kurdish town of Halabja
alternates.summary: On March 16, 1988, Iraqi forces attacked the Kurdish town of Halabja with chemical weapons, killing about 5,000 people.
alternates.significance: It was the deadliest chemical attack on civilians in history, but drew muted Western reaction at the time.
alternates.fbis: The Near East & South Asia Daily Report of March 17, 1988, shows a contents page, mostly unreadable in the OCR, that lists Iran-Iraq war items including Iraqi missiles hitting Dezful and "Halabjah 'Chemically Bombed'".
